questions.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=3x(t)-y(t)+5 \\ {y}^{′}(t)=2x(t)+y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of ODEs above. The equilibrium point of the system is $[-1,\,2]^{T}.$ Which of the following is the system obtained by shifting the equilibrium to the origin?
questions.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}=[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]x+[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 0\end{aligned}],
$$

where $x=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$

To shift the system's equilibrium from ${x}^{∗}$ to the origin, we define the deviation vector

$$
u=x-{x}^{∗},
$$

where $u=[\begin{aligned}u(t) \\ v(t)\end{aligned}].$

In our case, we have

$$
u=x-[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\,⇒\,x=u+[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\,\text{and}\,{x}^{′}={u}^{′}.
$$

Substituting $x$ and ${x}^{′}$ into the given system, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′} & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]x+[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ {u}^{′} & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}](u+[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}])+[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]u+[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]u+[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]u.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the shifted system is the following:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{u}^{′}(t)=3u(t)-v(t) \\ {v}^{′}(t)=2u(t)+v(t)\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ -1 & 4\end{aligned}]x+[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 9\end{aligned}],
$$

where $x=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$

To shift the system's equilibrium from ${x}^{∗}$ to the origin, we define the deviation vector

$$
u=x-{x}^{∗},
$$

where $u=[\begin{aligned}u(t) \\ v(t)\end{aligned}].$

In our case, we have

$$
u=x-[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}]\,⇒\,x=u+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}]\,\text{and}\,{x}^{′}={u}^{′}.
$$

Substituting $x$ and ${x}^{′}$ into the given system, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′} & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ -1 & 4\end{aligned}]x+[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 9\end{aligned}] \\ {u}^{′} & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ -1 & 4\end{aligned}](u+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}])+[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 9\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ -1 & 4\end{aligned}]u+[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ -1 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 9\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ -1 & 4\end{aligned}]u+[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ -9\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 9\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ -1 & 4\end{aligned}]u.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the shifted system is the following:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{u}^{′}(t)=2u(t)+3v(t) \\ {v}^{′}(t)=-u(t)+4v(t)\end{aligned}

questions.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)={x}^{2}(t)+4x(t)+y(t)+1 \\ {y}^{′}(t)=2x(t)-{y}^{2}(t)+8y(t)-10\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of ODEs above. An equilibrium point of the system is $[-1,\,2]^{T}.$ Which of the following is the system obtained by shifting this equilibrium to the origin?
questions.worked_solution:
To shift the system's equilibrium from ${x}^{∗}$ to the origin, we define the deviation vector

$$
u=x-{x}^{∗},
$$

where $x=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and $u=[\begin{aligned}u(t) \\ v(t)\end{aligned}].$

In our case, we have

$$
u=x-[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\,⇒\,x=u+[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\,\text{and}\,{x}^{′}={u}^{′}.
$$

In coordinate form, this can be written as follows:

$$
x(t)=u(t)-1,\,y(t)=v(t)+2,\,{x}^{′}(t)={u}^{′}(t),\,{v}^{′}(t)={y}^{′}(t).
$$

Let's now substitute these into the given system.

- Substituting into the first equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & ={x}^{2}(t)+4x(t)+y(t)+1 \\ {u}^{′}(t) & =(u(t)-1)^{2}+4(u(t)-1)+(v(t)+2)+1 \\  & =({u}^{2}(t)-2u(t)+1)+4u(t)-4+v(t)+2+1 \\  & ={u}^{2}(t)+2u(t)+v(t).\end{aligned}
$$

- Substituting into the second equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(t) & =2x(t)-{y}^{2}(t)+8y(t)-10 \\ {v}^{′}(t) & =2(u(t)-1)-(v(t)+2)^{2}+8(v(t)+2)-10 \\  & =2u(t)-2-({v}^{2}(t)+4v(t)+4)+8v(t)+16-10 \\  & =2u(t)-{v}^{2}(t)+4v(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the shifted system is the following:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{u}^{′}(t)={u}^{2}(t)+2u(t)+v(t) \\ {v}^{′}(t)=2u(t)-{v}^{2}(t)+4v(t)\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)={x}^{2}(t)-6x(t)+2y(t)+9 \\ {y}^{′}(t)=4x(t)-{y}^{2}(t)+y(t)-12\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of ODEs above. An equilibrium point of the system is $[3,\,0]^{T}.$ Which of the following is the system obtained by shifting this equilibrium to the origin?
questions.worked_solution:
To shift the system's equilibrium from ${x}^{∗}$ to the origin, we define the deviation vector

$$
u=x-{x}^{∗},
$$

where $x=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and $u=[\begin{aligned}u(t) \\ v(t)\end{aligned}].$

In our case, we have

$$
u=x-[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\,⇒\,x=u+[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\,\text{and}\,{x}^{′}={u}^{′}.
$$

In coordinate form, this can be written as follows:

$$
x(t)=u(t)+3,\,y(t)=v(t),\,{x}^{′}(t)={u}^{′}(t),\,{v}^{′}(t)={y}^{′}(t).
$$

Let's now substitute these into the given system.

- Substituting into the first equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & ={x}^{2}(t)-6x(t)+2y(t)+9 \\ {u}^{′}(t) & =(u(t)+3)^{2}-6(u(t)+3)+2v(t)+9 \\  & =({u}^{2}(t)+6u(t)+9)-6u(t)-18+2v(t)+9 \\  & ={u}^{2}(t)+2v(t).\end{aligned}
$$

- Substituting into the second equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(t) & =4x(t)-{y}^{2}(t)+y(t)-12 \\ {v}^{′}(t) & =4(u(t)+3)-{v}^{2}(t)+v(t)-12 \\  & =4u(t)+12-{v}^{2}(t)+v(t)-12 \\  & =4u(t)-{v}^{2}(t)+v(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the shifted system is the following:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{u}^{′}(t)={u}^{2}(t)+2v(t) \\ {v}^{′}(t)=4u(t)-{v}^{2}(t)+v(t)\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)={x}^{2}(t)-x(t)+y(t)-2 \\ {y}^{′}(t)=2x(t)-{y}^{2}(t)+3y(t)-2\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of ODEs above. An equilibrium point of the system is $[0,\,2]^{T}.$ Which of the following is the system obtained by shifting this equilibrium to the origin?
questions.worked_solution:
To shift the system's equilibrium from ${x}^{∗}$ to the origin, we define the deviation vector

$$
u=x-{x}^{∗},
$$

where $x=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and $u=[\begin{aligned}u(t) \\ v(t)\end{aligned}].$

In our case, we have

$$
u=x-[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\,⇒\,x=u+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\,\text{and}\,{x}^{′}={u}^{′}.
$$

In coordinate form, this can be written as follows:

$$
x(t)=u(t),\,y(t)=v(t)+2,\,{x}^{′}(t)={u}^{′}(t),\,{v}^{′}(t)={y}^{′}(t)
$$

Let's now substitute these into the given system.

- Substituting into the first equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & ={x}^{2}(t)-x(t)+y(t)-2 \\ {u}^{′}(t) & ={u}^{2}(t)-u(t)+(v(t)+2)-2 \\  & ={u}^{2}(t)-u(t)+v(t).\end{aligned}
$$

- Substituting into the second equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(t) & =2x(t)-{y}^{2}(t)+3y(t)-2 \\ {v}^{′}(t) & =2u(t)-(v(t)+2)^{2}+3(v(t)+2)-2 \\  & =2u(t)-({v}^{2}(t)+4v(t)+4)+3v(t)+6-2 \\  & =2u(t)-{v}^{2}(t)-v(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the shifted system is the following:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{u}^{′}(t)={u}^{2}(t)-u(t)+v(t) \\ {v}^{′}(t)=2u(t)-{v}^{2}(t)-v(t)\end{aligned}
$$

$$
x(t)=u(t)+1,\,y(t)=v(t)+1,\,{x}^{′}(t)={u}^{′}(t),\,{v}^{′}(t)={y}^{′}(t).

To shift the system's equilibrium from ${x}^{∗}$ to the origin, we define the deviation vector

$$
u=x-{x}^{∗},

where $x=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and $u=[\begin{aligned}u(t) \\ v(t)\end{aligned}].$

$$
x(t)=u(t)+1,\,y(t)=v(t)+2,\,{x}^{′}(t)={u}^{′}(t),\,{v}^{′}(t)={y}^{′}(t)

questions.problem: A linear system of ODEs has the equilibrium at ${x}^{∗}=[-2,\,4]^{T}.$ The eigenvalues of the system's matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2}.$ After shifting using $u=x-{x}^{∗},$ the system becomes ${u}^{′}=Au.$ Which of the following is **guaranteed** to be an eigenvalue of the matrix $A?$
questions.worked_solution:
After shifting a linear system, the eigenvalues and the corresponding eigenvectors remain unchanged.

Thus, the matrix $A$ in the shifted system has the same eigenvalues as the system's matrix in the original coordinates. These eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ or any expressions that are equal to them.

Among the given options, the only quantity that is guaranteed to be an eigenvalue of $A$ is ${\lambda }_{2}.$

questions.problem: A linear system of ODEs has an equilibrium at ${x}^{∗}.$ One of the nullclines of the system has the equation $y=2x-3$ in the corresponding phase space. The system is then shifted using $u=x-{x}^{∗}.$ Which of the following is **guaranteed** to be a nullcline of the shifted system?
questions.worked_solution:
After shifting a system, the geometric structure of the vector field is preserved. In particular, each nullcline is translated but retains its orientation, meaning its slope does not change.

Because the equilibrium is moved to the origin by the shift, the translated nullclines must pass through the origin in the shifted coordinates.

Thus, the nullclines of the shifted system pass through the origin and have the same slopes as the corresponding nullclines of the original system.

Among the given options, the only line that satisfied the above conditions is $y=2x.$

questions.problem: A nonlinear system of ODEs has exactly two equilibrium points. The system is then shifted using the transformation $u=x-{x}^{∗},$ where ${x}^{∗}$ is one of the equilibria. Which of the following statements about the number of equilibria in the shifted system is guaranteed to be true?
questions.worked_solution:
A shift of coordinates is a translation of the phase space and does not alter the structure of the system’s equilibrium set. Each equilibrium point of the original system is translated to a corresponding equilibrium in the shifted coordinates.

Thus, although one of the equilibria is moved to the origin, the total number of equilibrium points remains the same.

Therefore, the correct answer is "The shifted system still has exactly two equilibrium points."

questions.problem: A system of ODEs has a stable star node at ${x}^{∗}.$ The system is then shifted using $u=x-{x}^{∗}.$ Which of the following best describes the point $(0,0)$ for the shifted system?
questions.worked_solution:
Shifting does not alter the local behavior near an equilibrium. So, the equilibrium retains its original classification (saddle, node, spiral, center, etc.).

Recall that the shift moves the equilibrium to the origin.

Thus, the equilibrium at $(0,0)$ in the shifted system has the same classification as ${x}^{∗}$ in the original system.

Therefore, the correct answer is "A stable star node".

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=3x(t)-2y(t)+1 \\ {y}^{′}(t)=4x(t)+y(t)-6\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of ODEs above. The equilibrium point of the system is $[1, \, 2]^T.$ What is the system obtained by shifting the equilibrium to the origin?
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069931/assets/2c994a3f48f4d9e12a179b03538977f72e033c5e539ec6f73c6d4529c1674299.png)
where ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069931/assets/d1aac4dbbbd1d7579a0a03c1440b3140efc18f43d6a8016e867e9419af693675.png)

To shift the system's equilibrium from $\mathbf{x}^\ast$ to the origin, we define the deviation vector

$$
\mathbf{u} 
= \mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}^\ast,
$$

where ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069931/assets/6118cf06e6accf9f29665d66c4c4d00e0e7e2eb8bdbd98bd9044ee418422ca59.png)

In our case, we have
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069931/assets/fb0d2631e167027b68263b62af5ba65d91442fdc89d1c16e39d6299f97835307.png)

Substituting $\mathbf{x}$ and $\mathbf{x}'$ into the given system, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′} & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ 4 & 1\end{aligned}]x+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -6\end{aligned}] \\ {u}^{′} & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ 4 & 1\end{aligned}](u+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}])+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ 4 & 1\end{aligned}]u+[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ 4 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ 4 & 1\end{aligned}]u+[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 6\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ 4 & 1\end{aligned}]u.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the shifted system is the following:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{u}^{′}(t)=3u(t)-2v(t) \\ {v}^{′}(t)=4u(t)+v(t)\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Shifting the Equilibrium to the Origin: Non-Linear Systems
canonical_examples.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)={x}^{2}(t)+x(t)+y(t)+2 \\ {y}^{′}(t)=5x(t)-{y}^{2}(t)+3y(t)+10\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of ODEs above. An equilibrium point of the system is $[0, \, -2]^T.$ What system is obtained by shifting this equilibrium to the origin?
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To shift the system's equilibrium from $\mathbf{x}^\ast$ to the origin, we define the deviation vector

$$
\mathbf{u} 
= \mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}^\ast,
$$

where ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069931/assets/951509e719a40caba7ecc5872d983b6cf83128d77af670c88846d2a06d329d8e.png) and ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069931/assets/a3d02714f52ce42ec3e6d78d9cdd91f4c2ca14a59948f078d93318c94ec5e31a.png)

In our case, we have
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069931/assets/cce8b4b07839490b3be0841f8a4e6e73b69426426504625cedecf738947b046d.png)

In coordinate form, this can be written as follows:

$$
x(t) = u(t), \qquad
y(t) = v(t) - 2, \qquad
x'(t) = u'(t), \qquad
v'(t) = y'(t).
$$

Let's now substitute these into the given system.

- Substituting into the first equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & ={x}^{2}(t)+x(t)+y(t)+2 \\ {u}^{′}(t) & ={u}^{2}(t)+u(t)+(v(t)-2)+2 \\  & ={u}^{2}(t)+u(t)+v(t).\end{aligned}
$$

- Substituting into the second equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(t) & =5x(t)-{y}^{2}(t)+3y(t)+10 \\ {v}^{′}(t) & =5u(t)-(v(t)-2)^{2}+3(v(t)-2)+10 \\  & =5u(t)-({v}^{2}(t)-4v(t)+4)+3v(t)-6+10 \\  & =5u(t)-{v}^{2}(t)+7v(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the shifted system is the following:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{u}^{′}(t)={u}^{2}(t)+u(t)+v(t) \\ {v}^{′}(t)=5u(t)-{v}^{2}(t)+7v(t)\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Identifying Properties of a Shifted System
canonical_examples.problem:
A linear system of ODEs has an equilibrium at $\mathbf{x}^\ast.$ One of the nullclines of the system has the equation $y=3x-1$ in the corresponding phase space. The system is then shifted using $\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}^\ast.$ Which of the following is **guaranteed** to be a nullcline of the shifted system?

- $y=3x+3$

- $y=-x$

- $y=3x$

- $y=-3x$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
After shifting a system, the geometric structure of the vector field is preserved. In particular, each nullcline is translated but retains its orientation, meaning its slope does not change.

Because the equilibrium is moved to the origin by the shift, the translated nullclines must pass through the origin in the shifted coordinates.

Thus, the nullclines of the shifted system pass through the origin and have the same slopes as the corresponding nullclines of the original system.

Among the given options, the only line that satisfied the above conditions is $y=3x.$
